stories.headline: Update: CENTCOM Commander Advised Halting Hormuz Bombing as U.S. Pauses Iran Strikes
stories.summary:
The top U.S. military commander in the Middle East, Adm. Brad Cooper of CENTCOM, recommended stopping the bombing campaign around the Strait of Hormuz, advising that it had reached the limit of its effectiveness, according to two sources with direct knowledge of his position. His recommendation, along with input from other advisers, was a significant factor in President Trump's decision Friday to pause U.S. airstrikes against Iran. Four U.S. soldiers were killed in the region last week as the conflict escalated, and Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth attended a dignified transfer ceremony Wednesday.

The new reporting provides the clearest inside account yet of the military deliberations behind the pause in strikes, adding a concrete new development to a fast-moving situation. The U.S. military separately reported firing on a merchant vessel attempting to breach its blockade of Iranian ports — the second commercial ship disabled since the blockade was reimposed in the Strait of Hormuz.

Meanwhile, Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels said they fired missiles and drones at Saudi Arabia in response to Saudi airstrikes on the Red Sea port city of Hodeida, targeting Aramco facilities in Yanbu and Jizan. Saudi Arabia's civil defense confirmed alerts sounded in both cities but offered no further comment. The Houthis have threatened to close the Bab el-Mandeb Strait to Saudi-linked shipping entirely unless the blockade on Yemen is lifted.

The Bab el-Mandeb, at the southern tip of the Arabian Peninsula, handles roughly 12 percent of global trade and a quarter of container traffic. Iran's foreign minister called for diplomacy, while President Trump said the U.S. remains "locked and loaded" even as he described ongoing negotiations as "serious."

stories.headline: Laura Loomer Reverses on Ukraine Aid After Kyiv Visit, Signaling Possible Shift in MAGA Base
stories.summary:
Laura Loomer, one of President Trump's most influential outside political allies, publicly reversed her longstanding opposition to U.S. military aid to Ukraine following a visit to the country last week. After touring bombed neighborhoods and meeting with Ukrainian officials including President Volodymyr Zelensky, Loomer posted a series of messages on X calling for "moral clarity" on Russia's conduct and distancing herself from skeptics within the GOP. "I don't care if people in the GOP disavow me," she wrote. "They will come to see how evil Russia is."

The reversal carries unusual political weight because of Loomer's documented influence within Trump's inner circle. Trump amplified a clip of Loomer's interview with Zelensky on Truth Social Thursday, writing simply "very good!!!!" Senior Trump administration officials told the Washington Examiner that the shift could reinforce the president's own evolving position on the conflict. "She has his ear," one senior official said.

Trump has steadily signaled growing support for Ukraine in recent months, with allies noting he has been impressed by Ukraine's domestic defense industry expansion and its drone campaign against Russian targets. Trump recently announced the U.S. would grant licenses for Ukraine to produce its own Patriot missiles and is scheduled to host Zelensky at the White House this week — a visit that will be closely watched given the diplomatic backdrop.

Loomer has never held a government position but has exercised notable personnel influence; following a private meeting with Trump and Vice President JD Vance last April, several national security aides she criticized were subsequently dismissed. Her shift on Ukraine is the latest signal that the America First wing of the GOP may be moving toward a harder line against Russia as the conflict continues.

stories.headline: Update: U.S. Pauses Iran Airstrikes as Diplomacy Advances; Houthis Strike Saudi Arabia
stories.summary:
The United States military has paused its nearly two-week campaign of airstrikes against Iran, with diplomatic efforts accelerating in an attempt to avert a return to full-scale conflict. Iran's Foreign Ministry confirmed that Tehran and Oman held several rounds of technical talks in Iran over the weekend regarding Strait of Hormuz transit arrangements. A regional official involved in mediation said both sides want to return to the interim ceasefire deal, with a compromise centered on allowing vessel transit through the strait under fewer restrictions.

President Trump described the U.S. as "locked and loaded" while also saying "serious" negotiations are continuing — a characteristically mixed signal that has left analysts uncertain whether the pause represents a strategic inflection point or merely an operational break. Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu is expected to visit Washington next week, adding another variable; Israel, which launched the conflict alongside the U.S. in February, has been absent from the latest round of strikes. Some analysts suggest Israel's restraint may itself be a diplomatic signal to Tehran.

Meanwhile, Yemen's Houthi rebels escalated regional tensions by firing missiles and drones at Saudi Arabia's Yanbu and Jizan cities — both home to major Aramco oil facilities — in retaliation for Saudi airstrikes on the Red Sea port of Hodeida. Saudi Arabia's civil defense confirmed alerts sounded in both cities but offered no further comment. The Houthis have threatened to close the Bab el-Mandeb Strait to Saudi-linked shipping unless the kingdom ends its blockade of Yemen.

The U.S. military also separately disclosed it fired on a merchant vessel attempting to breach its blockade of Iranian ports — the second commercial ship disabled since the reimposition of the Strait of Hormuz blockade. Brent crude fell 3.9% on Friday to $96.78 after briefly topping $100, though analysts warn energy markets have diminished buffers if escalation resumes. The Federal Reserve meets next week with rising inflation and potential rate increases looming over an already stressed global economy.

stories.headline: Update: Ukraine War — New Developments as Conflict Enters Latest Phase
stories.summary:
Coverage of Russia's ongoing invasion of Ukraine continues across more than two dozen major outlets, reflecting sustained global attention to a conflict now in its fifth year. The war remains one of the most widely tracked ongoing stories in international journalism, with implications for European security, NATO cohesion, global grain and energy markets, and the broader post-Cold War international order.

Recent weeks have seen Ukraine expand drone operations targeting Russian logistics infrastructure, including the Wildberries campaign hitting multiple hubs. Meanwhile, Romania earlier this week shot down a drone over its airspace in the first-ever NATO interception, marking a significant escalation in the conflict's reach toward alliance territory. Ukraine's ousted defence minister has also refused an alternative post and demanded reinstatement, pointing to ongoing political tensions within Kyiv's wartime government.

The conflict continues to draw the diplomatic attention of European capitals and Washington, even as the U.S. administration remains heavily focused on its confrontation with Iran. Western military and humanitarian aid pipelines remain central to Ukraine's ability to sustain operations. No ceasefire negotiations are currently active.

stories.headline: Trump Makes 2028 Run Announcement, Touts Term Limits at Rescheduled WHCA Dinner
stories.summary:
President Donald Trump delivered a marathon, roughly one-hour speech Friday at the rescheduled White House Correspondents' Association Dinner, the event having been postponed after a gunman breached security at the original April gathering. Trump opened with a unifying message about political violence, saying the country "settles differences with open and vigorous debate" and praising Secret Service agent Victor Gonzalez, who stopped the attacker. He also made several jokes about the press and members of his own administration, including quipping that his original, pre-assassination-attempt remarks would have been far harsher toward journalists.

Trump used the speech to float several policy and political positions, most prominently announcing his intention to seek a fourth term in 2028 — donning a red 'Trump 2028' cap as the crowd reacted — while simultaneously calling for congressional term limits, a contrast that drew immediate comment. He also repeated claims that the 2020 election was rigged, calling his loss to Joe Biden invalid. The announcements were widely covered, with 17 outlets reporting on the speech.

Supporters characterized the address as a return to form — confident, combative in places, and occasionally self-deprecating — while critics noted the speech veered between unifying rhetoric and partisan attacks. The 2028 comment is legally contested given the 22nd Amendment's two-term limit, and the White House had not clarified whether Trump views it as a serious declaration or a rhetorical flourish.

The event itself featured enhanced security measures and a smaller crowd than typical WHCA gatherings, reflecting ongoing concerns following the April attack. Trump's attendance marked a departure from recent presidential tradition of skipping the dinner entirely.

stories.headline: New UK Prime Minister Burnham Pledges to Challenge Trump Publicly if Required
stories.summary:
New United Kingdom Prime Minister Andy Burnham, in his first major broadcast interview since taking office, pledged to defend British national interests and to publicly disagree with U.S. President Donald Trump when necessary. Burnham described his initial contact with Trump as "really warm" but made clear that warmth would not preclude open disagreement on matters of national concern.

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting reinforced the message, saying the Trump administration is not seeking allies who "suck up" but rather those confident enough to state disagreements plainly. The comments signal Burnham intends a more assertive posture than some predecessors in managing the transatlantic relationship.

The statement carries particular significance given ongoing U.S.-UK trade negotiations and the broader backdrop of strained relations between Washington and European capitals over tariffs and NATO burden-sharing. Burnham's positioning attempts to balance maintaining the special relationship while appealing to a domestic audience skeptical of deference to Washington.

stories.headline: Hearing Reveals Singer D4vd Allegedly Began Sexual Contact with Victim When She Was 11
stories.summary:
A Los Angeles court held a preliminary hearing Friday to determine whether singer D4vd, legally named David Anthony Burke, should stand trial for the murder of 14-year-old Celeste Rivas Hernandez. Prosecutors presented iCloud data showing text messages between Burke and Celeste dating back to August 2022, when she was 11 years old and he was 17, as well as photos prosecutors allege depict sexual abuse.

Text messages shown in court revealed that Celeste had become pregnant and undergone at least two abortions before her death. In one exchange from January 2024, Burke asked if the child was his; in another from June 2024, he wrote "Let's let this abortion be the last one." Prosecutors allege Burke killed Celeste after she threatened to expose the relationship and destroy his career. He has pleaded not guilty to murder and sexual abuse charges.

Forensic testimony from the Los Angeles County medical examiner noted it was "extremely difficult" to pinpoint the exact time of death due to decomposition, a point the defense seized on to suggest alternative explanations. DNA from blood found in Burke's Hollywood Hills home matched Celeste, according to police testimony. The hearing will determine whether the case proceeds to trial.

stories.headline: Left-Wing Democrats Win Primaries but Face Test of Electability With Swing Voters Ahead of Midterms
stories.summary:
Progressive Democrats have recorded a string of primary victories this summer — including in New York and Colorado — but now face a pivotal test of whether their platform can attract the working-class voters who shifted to Donald Trump in 2024. The tension is playing out most visibly in Michigan, where Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, championed by Senators Bernie Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, is locked in a tight Democratic primary against moderate Congresswoman Haley Stevens ahead of an August 4 vote.

El-Sayed is running on Medicare for All, opposition to immigration enforcement, and staunch opposition to U.S. aid to Israel. Stevens, backed by Governor Gretchen Whitmer and outgoing Senator Gary Peters, has positioned herself as the more electable candidate with a proven fundraising base and centrist appeal. The open Michigan Senate seat is considered a must-win for Democrats seeking to claw back Senate influence.

Some Democratic voters at a Saturday rally expressed optimism that progressive energy could power turnout, while others outside the venue were more cautious. "This may not be the moment for progressives," said one 74-year-old likely Stevens voter, who said electability should take priority over ideological purity given the stakes. The broader battle reflects an unresolved internal Democratic debate about whether moving left wins back disillusioned workers or accelerates their drift to Republicans.

The outcome of the Michigan primary and similar contests in other battleground states will be closely watched as both parties calibrate their strategies ahead of the November midterms.

stories.headline: Update: Berlin Pride Attacker Identified as Islamist-Linked Suspect; Manhunt Underway After One Killed, 16 Injured
stories.summary:
A vehicle was driven into crowds attending Berlin's Christopher Street Day Pride event late Saturday night, killing one woman and injuring 16 others. The attack occurred at approximately 10 p.m. local time in Tiergarten park, near the Brandenburg Gate, where hundreds of thousands had gathered for the annual celebration. Several victims were also stabbed during the incident, and the Pride event was cancelled immediately afterward.

Berlin police identified the suspect as 21-year-old Abdul B., whose surname is withheld under German law. By early Sunday morning, authorities had located the vehicle used in the attack — found crashed into a tree — and identified the suspect as having connections to Islamist circles. A city-wide manhunt involving thousands of officers, including reinforcements from surrounding German states, is ongoing. Police warned the public not to approach the suspect, who is believed to be armed and dangerous.

Authorities said one or more additional individuals may have fled the vehicle, raising the possibility of multiple suspects. Police released an image of Abdul B. and called on the public for information. The attack is the latest in a series of vehicle-ramming incidents at public gatherings in Europe and is likely to intensify political debates in Germany over Islamist radicalization and security at large public events.

This is a developing story. A previous item covered earlier reports of injuries at the Berlin Pride event; the new developments include the confirmed fatality, the suspect's identification, the Islamist link, and the active manhunt.

stories.headline: Federal Appeals Court Blocks Trump Mail-In Voting Order Ahead of Midterms
stories.summary:
The U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit on Saturday declined to lift a lower-court injunction blocking key provisions of President Trump's executive order on mail-in voting, leaving the restrictions unenforceable in 23 states ahead of November's midterm elections. The ruling upholds a June decision by a Boston federal judge who found parts of the order unlawful. The Justice Department had signaled it may seek emergency relief from the Supreme Court if it did not prevail at the appellate level.

The executive order had sought to impose stricter requirements on mail-in ballots, a change the administration framed as necessary to safeguard election integrity ahead of midterms in which control of both chambers of Congress is at stake. Critics, including the Democratic-led states that secured the original injunction, argued the order exceeded presidential authority and would disenfranchise millions of voters who rely on mail-in balloting.

The ruling sets up a potential Supreme Court showdown with the midterms approaching. Supporters of the order, primarily Republicans, argue that tightening mail-in rules reduces fraud and restores public confidence in elections. Opponents, largely Democrats, contend the restrictions are a form of voter suppression with no documented fraud problem to justify them.

The case is one of several legal battles shaping the electoral landscape heading into November, with both parties watching closely for any Supreme Court intervention that could alter voting procedures across the country.

stories.headline: Hawaii Lt. Governor Sylvia Luke Indicted on 12-Count Bribery Charge
stories.summary:
Hawaii Lieutenant Governor Sylvia Luke, a Democrat, was indicted Friday on 12 counts of bribery following a monthslong state investigation into a campaign finance scandal. A Hawaii grand jury alleged that Luke accepted campaign contributions in 2022, while she was still a state lawmaker, in exchange for securing government funding for COVID-19 testing sites. The alleged bribe totaled approximately $35,000 tied to a COVID-19 testing contract.

Governor Josh Green publicly called for Luke's resignation following the indictment. The charges represent a significant legal and political crisis for Hawaii's Democratic-led state government. Luke has not yet entered a public plea in response to the indictment.

The case adds to a broader national pattern of public corruption investigations at the state level and is notable given Luke's prominence as a top elected official in Hawaii. It may also create political complications for the state Democratic Party ahead of the November elections.

stories.headline: Markets Post Second Straight Losing Week as Iran War, Tariffs, and Inflation Weigh on Investors
stories.summary:
U.S. stock markets finished mixed Friday but logged a second consecutive losing week — the first back-to-back weekly decline since March — as the escalating U.S.-Iran war, fresh tariffs on 60 trading partners, and persistent inflation dampened investor confidence. The S&P 500 barely moved on Friday, while the Nasdaq fell 0.6%, dragged down by losses in large technology stocks including Micron Technology, which dropped 7%, and Broadcom, which fell 2.7%.

Oil prices fell for the first time in a week, with Brent crude dropping 3.9% to $96.78 per barrel after briefly surpassing $100 on Thursday. Before the Iran war began in late February, Brent was trading around $72. Heavy fighting in the Middle East has repeatedly threatened global oil flows, and analysts warn that energy markets now have less resilience than earlier in the year, with U.S. strategic reserves already drawn down.

The Federal Reserve is set to meet next week amid rising concern that new tariffs and elevated energy prices could reignite inflation, complicating the central bank's path on interest rates. Wall Street had hoped for a rate cut this year; expectations have since shifted toward a potential rate increase. The combination of geopolitical uncertainty, trade policy disruption, and inflationary pressure is creating a challenging environment for markets and the broader economy heading into the second half of 2026.
